rationale: Round 1 built, ran correctly, and hit no ICE fallback, so this round pushes obfuscation strength up across all seven passes while keeping cost and risk weights below the security weights. BCF gets the highest SecurityGain since bogus control flow is the strongest deterrent against static control-flow recovery and this program's tiny text size (1359 bytes, largest function 230 bytes) leaves ample headroom for its size inflation; FLA and IGV follow closely to flatten the branchy trie_insert/trie_scan loops and obscure global state (trie root, charsequence cursor), which are the natural reverse-engineering anchors in this benchmark. IBR and ICALL are weighted high to convert direct branches and calls into indirect dispatch, compounding with FLA so flattened dispatchers are not trivially re-linked. SUB and SPLIT carry strong but slightly lower weights because they are cheap, low-risk passes that layer instruction-level diversity on top of the structural transforms. Cost and risk weights are held in the 0.25-0.55 band: high enough that the feature-driven selector still applies passes to hot functions (trie_scan, trie_insert, charsequence_push) where runtime matters, but never dominant, since the round-1 measurement showed no correctness or build issues and the goal now is to trade some of that headroom for resistance rather than leave it unspent.
